newsitem.title: UK: Small UK jobless fall shows rate rise was rash-TUC.
newsitem.headline: Small UK jobless fall shows rate rise was rash-TUC.

text.p: A modest fall in British unemployment in May shows last week's rate rise was premature, the Trades Union Congress said on Wednesday.
Although unemployment fell to a seven-year low the dole queues were only cut by 18,400 last month, well below the 50-60,000 drops seen in recent months.

"Any fall in unemployment is welcome. But what this modest fall in unemployment and current stable earnings growth clearly show is that last week's interest rate rise was premature," said John Monks, the TUC's General Secretary, said.
Underlying average earnings growth was steady at 4.5 percent in the year to March.
Last Friday, Britain's new monetary policy committee raised base rates by a quarter-point to 6.25 percent at its very first meeting.
Monks said Wednesday's jobless figures showed previous falls were exaggerated by the Jobseekers Allowance.

The JSA was introduced last year and toughened up the rules covering eligibility for unemployment benefit. The switch to a new system caused a huge backlog of claims that went unprocessed, causing unemployment totals to look smaller than they actually were.
But the Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday that effect had unwound -- the claimant account is no longer being distorted by the JSA.
"Today's figures give a clearer picture of the underlying fall in claimant unemployment because the Jobseekers Allowance effect has dropped out," Monks said.
"Young people and the long-term unemployed are still not enjoying even these modest benefits of our economic recovery.

"These two groups desperately need the kind of measures proposed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown under his New Deal scheme aimed at getting people off benefits and into jobs," he said.
Brown has pledged to levy a windfall tax on Britain's privatised utilities in his first budget on July 2. The proceeds will be used to get 250,000 young people and long-term unemployed into work.
